name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Saturday 28 July 1973

clue.text: Dreamily perceived fault in Isaacson's hose

definitions.note: a participle phrase standing for the thing seen in a dream

blocks.note: first meaning: the stairway to heaven that Jacob saw in a dream in Genesis
second meaning: Isaac's son was Jacob, and a fault running down a stocking is a ladder

explanation.surface: Someone half-asleep spots a flaw in the stockings of a man called Isaacson.
explanation.walkthrough: Isaacson is split as Isaac's son, who is Jacob. A ladder is the British word for a run in tights or stockings.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis, Jacob dreams of a stairway reaching up to heaven with angels on it, which is called Jacob's ladder.

blocks.note: surface reading: a noisy town with thin walls
setter's reading: Biblical walls that fell when priests blew their trumpets, so plainly not proof against sound

explanation.walkthrough: In the Book of Joshua, the walls of this ancient city came tumbling down at a blast of trumpets and a shout.
explanation.definitionFit: Joshua's siege of the ancient city in the Bible ended when its walls fell to the sound of trumpets.

clue.text: Firm came to terms with British aircraft

blocks.note: Co. is the abbreviation for company
met as in met the terms, satisfied them

explanation.surface: A company has reached a deal with a British aircraft maker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' looks like an adjective; it is a noun, a business.
explanation.definitionFit: The de Havilland Comet was the first commercial jet airliner, built in Britain.

blocks.note: surface reading: a sensual versifier
setter's reading: the poet in Gilbert and Sullivan's opera Patience, who loses the milkmaid Patience

explanation.walkthrough: Reginald, the 'fleshly poet' of Gilbert and Sullivan's Patience, fails to win the title heroine, so he literally loses Patience.
explanation.definitionFit: In the comic opera the aesthetic poet is called a fleshly poet and ends the show without the girl.

clue.text: Was inclined, say, to be fast

indicators.note: say asks us to speak the words and take the spelling of a word with that sound

blocks.note: was inclined means tilted or sloped

explanation.surface: Someone felt disposed to go without food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Was inclined' suggests a mood; it means physically sloped, which is leant in British spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Lent is the forty days before Easter when Christians traditionally fast.

clue.text: A hell of a beauty-spot? That's the message

blocks.note: Dis is the Roman underworld, and so hell
a patch was a small piece of silk worn on the face as a beauty spot

explanation.surface: A cheeky postcard from an awful tourist spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A hell of a beauty-spot' reads as a dreadful scenic place; the beauty spot is the cosmetic kind.
explanation.definitionFit: A dispatch is an official report or message sent quickly, often by a correspondent or envoy.

clue.text: They have a hangover on the house

definitions.text: They have a hangover on the house

blocks.note: surface reading: drinkers suffering after free drinks, on the house
setter's reading: parts of a roof that overhang the walls of a building

explanation.walkthrough: 'On the house' means free drinks, but here it is literal: the edge of the roof projects beyond the walls.
explanation.definitionFit: The lower edges of a roof that project beyond the walls are an overhang on a building.

blocks.note: sc. is an abbreviation for science, as in BSc
a ramble is a leisurely country walk

explanation.surface: Setting off on a nature walk with a scientific purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take off' suggests leaving or undressing; here it is fighter planes taking off in a hurry.
explanation.definitionFit: Military aircraft scramble when they are ordered to take off at once to meet a threat.

indicators.note: out can mean disordered or wrong, so the letters do not stay in place

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone made a spider leave its hiding place.
explanation.definitionFit: Prised means levered open by force, as a lid is prised off with a tool.

clue.text: They chew things over, indicating spirit in workers

blocks.note: rum is a spirit distilled from sugar cane
taken as written
worker ants are the classic crossword workers

explanation.surface: A comment that people who brood over things are drinkers among the workforce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like it asks for one piece inside another, but it simply supplies its own two letters between the others.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruminants such as cattle bring food back up from the stomach and chew it a second time.

blocks.note: six in Roman numerals
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone from Wakefield who owns a six-cylinder car.
explanation.walkthrough: Wakefield is split into two words so it looks like a place; it points to Goldsmith's novel The Vicar of Wakefield.
explanation.definitionFit: The title character of Oliver Goldsmith's novel is the clergyman Dr Primrose, the Vicar of Wakefield.

blocks.note: surface reading: a melody that sticks in the head
setter's reading: anglers want a catch, so a tune for them would be named after their haul

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the pun: a fisherman's tune would be one full of catches.
explanation.definitionFit: A tune that is easy to pick up and remember is called catchy in everyday speech.

definitions.note: an adjective standing for the noun: light breezes

blocks.note: first meaning: a cat's-paw is a light breeze that ruffles calm water
second meaning: in the fable a monkey uses a cat's paw to pull roasting chestnuts from the fire

explanation.walkthrough: A cat's-paw has come to mean a dupe used to do someone else's dirty work, from the fable of the chestnuts.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors call small ripples raised by a light wind on still water cat's-paws, and the fable gives the second sense.

definitions.note: the material for basketwork rather than the work itself

indicators.note: something involved is tangled up, so the letters are twisted into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A rose has been woven into a piece of wickerwork.
explanation.definitionFit: Osiers are willow shoots, the pliable rods traditionally woven into baskets.

indicators.note: becoming means turning into something else, so the letters turn into a new word

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone admits that the more ratty they become, the more they annoy others.
explanation.walkthrough: Ratty is British slang for bad-tempered, which suits the surface perfectly.
explanation.definitionFit: To irritate someone is to annoy them, which is exactly causing them vexation.

definitions.note: a present participle; the answer is a past participle

blocks.note: first meaning: called off, as a launch or event is
second meaning: cleaned something out by rubbing hard

explanation.surface: An event was rained off and the whole thing was a washout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Washout' suggests a rained-off event, matching the first half; here it means a literal washing out.
explanation.definitionFit: To scrub a plan is informal for cancelling it, while scrubbing is also hard washing with a brush.

blocks.note: first meaning: to emphasise, as by drawing a rule beneath words
second meaning: sailors call the equator the Line, so south of it is below that line

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the strain of the tropics, but the second half is read as two words: under the Line.
explanation.definitionFit: To underline a point is to emphasise it, just as underlined text stands out on the page.

definitions.note: the answer is the adjective describing the hat

blocks.note: surface reading: something in the style of King Lear
setter's reading: Edward Lear wrote of himself that he wore a hat of a nonsense kind he invented

explanation.walkthrough: Lear here is Edward Lear, the nonsense poet, not the king; in 'How pleasant to know Mr Lear' he says he 'weareth a runcible hat'.
explanation.definitionFit: Runcible is a made-up word coined by Edward Lear, applied to a hat in his self-portrait poem.

blocks.note: first meaning: Cheddar in Somerset is famous for its gorge, so like it means full of gorge
second meaning: beautiful or magnificent

explanation.walkthrough: Cheddar looks like the cheese; it is the village with Cheddar Gorge, a limestone ravine in England, and the question mark flags the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: Gorgeous means strikingly beautiful or magnificent, as splendid does.

clue.text: Make a monkey out of the historian

blocks.note: first meaning: a small long-armed ape, loosely a monkey
second meaning: Edward ... wrote The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire

explanation.surface: Someone sets out to ridicule a scholar of history.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make a monkey out of' is an idiom for making someone look foolish; here it means turning the historian's name into an animal.
explanation.definitionFit: The gibbon is a tree-swinging ape of south-east Asia, loosely called a monkey.

blocks.note: first meaning: a formal verb meaning to turn attention to a subject
second meaning: a short form of advertisement in a newspaper

explanation.walkthrough: The verb sense is rare, as in 'he adverted to the matter'; the question mark admits that an advertisement is a loose kind of announcement.
explanation.definitionFit: To advert to something is to mention it, and an advert is the British shortening of advertisement.

clue.text: To type, getting money, is of current interest

blocks.note: taken as written
pica is a size of printing type
L stands for the pound, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: Typing for pay is in fashion these days.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Type' looks like a verb about keyboards; it is the printer's noun, and pica is a standard type size.
explanation.definitionFit: Topical matters relate to present events, the subjects people are currently interested in.

blocks.note: surface reading: perhaps a vehicle belonging to someone named Ariel
setter's reading: Ariel, the spirit in The Tempest, sings of flying after summer on a small creature

explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare's sprite sings 'On the bat's back I do fly / After summer merrily', so after summer means autumn.
explanation.definitionFit: Ariel's song in The Tempest names the creature he rides once summer is over.

definitions.note: a gambling game rather than the act of gambling

blocks.note: b is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for bowled
taken as written
the 'to' is dropped, leaving the verb itself

explanation.surface: A batsman dismissed in cricket heads off to place some bets.
explanation.walkthrough: Bowled is how a batsman is out in cricket when the ball hits the stumps; scorecards write it as b.
explanation.definitionFit: Bingo is a game of chance played for money prizes, a popular form of gambling.

blocks.note: first meaning: to occur unexpectedly
second meaning: read literally, a harvest that goes up

explanation.surface: A farmer hopes chance will bring a bigger harvest.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that crops up arises or occurs without warning, while a crop that goes up is a bigger yield.

clue.text: Plus four at dinner? How tasty!

definitions.text: Plus four at dinner? How tasty!

blocks.note: surface reading: the baggy golfing trousers called plus fours
setter's reading: the French word for small that goes before four in the name of tiny cakes served after dinner

explanation.walkthrough: Plus fours are knee-length golfing breeches; swap the first word for the French one and you have petits fours, the little cakes with coffee.
explanation.definitionFit: Petit is French for small, the first word of petit four, a bite-sized cake or sweet.

indicators.note: in a down answer an ascent climbs upward, so the letters are read from bottom to top

blocks.note: the compass abbreviation
an alp is a high mountain, as in the Swiss Alps

explanation.surface: A route is being mapped out for climbing a northern peak.
explanation.definitionFit: A plan and a scheme are both an arrangement worked out in advance for doing something.

blocks.note: first meaning: decimal means based on ten
second meaning: the adverb for something happening many times

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a recurring decimal in arithmetic; instead the answer is split into two words that describe a decimal system.
explanation.definitionFit: Often means many times, which is the adverb answering how frequently something recurs.

definitions.note: an adjective sense: relating to projectiles

indicators.note: the extra letters are placed in the middle of the sea's name

blocks.note: taken as written
fifty in Roman numerals
taken as written

explanation.surface: A naval report: fifty missiles are somewhere in the Baltic Sea.
explanation.walkthrough: The insert goes after the first three letters of the sea's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Ballistic describes the science and flight of objects that are thrown or fired, so it works as projectile.

clue.text: To control the intellectual describes the state's business

blocks.note: to govern is to rule or control
mental means of the mind or intellect

explanation.surface: Taming the clever people is what the business of the state is all about.
explanation.definitionFit: Governmental is the adjective used for anything concerning the running of the state.
